CALL AND NOTICE OF SPECIAL MEETING

  To the Members of the City Council of the City of Palos Verdes Estates:

  NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Mayor has called a special meeting of the City
  Council to take place in the Gallery Room of the Malaga Cove Library, 2400 Vía
  Campesina, Palos Verdes Estates, CA at 6:30 P.M. on Thursday, January 25, 2018. The
  agenda for the special meeting with the items of business to be transacted or discussed is set
  forth below.

  Posted by the Office of the City Clerk on January 24, 2018, at 5:00 p.m.

  January 25, 2018
  6:30 P.M. – 8:30 P.M.
  Malaga Cove Library, Gallery Room
  2400 Vía Campesina
  Palos Verdes Estates

  AGENDA
  OF A SPECIAL MEETING
  OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  PALOS VERDES ESTATES, CALIFORNIA

Copies of the staff reports or other written documentation relating to each item of business
referred to on the agenda are on file in the office of the City Clerk and are available for public
inspection. If applicable, materials related to an item on this agenda submitted to the Council
after distribution of the agenda packet are available for public inspection in the City Clerk’s office
during normal business hours. Any person having any question concerning any agenda item may
call the City Clerk to make inquiry concerning the item. Upon request, the agenda and
documents in the agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to
persons with a disability in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act. Please
contact the City Clerk at 310-378-0383, at least 48 hours prior to the meeting to request a
disability-related modification or accommodation.

 The City Council welcomes and encourages public participation at the Council meetings;
however, to allow for the orderly progression of business, each person wishing to comment or
make a presentation shall be limited to up to three (3) minutes. Anyone wishing to address the
City Council is requested to fill out a green speaker’s card available at the end of each row in
the Chambers. The card permits the City to identify persons for purposes of City Council
minute preparation. The City Council, at the direction of the Mayor with concurrence of the
Council, may modify the order of items shown on the agenda.

NEW BUSINESS

This is a workshop for information sharing and discussion between members of the City
Council, Planning Commission and Palos Verdes Homes Association; no actions will be taken.

1.  Status and Deliverables from the City/Palos Verdes Homes Association Ad Hoc Committee
  Regarding:

  a.  Residential Development Process Flow
  b.  Impact Assessment Tool for Planning Commission Review

  Garage Size, Size of Each Floor, etc.).

2.  Consideration of Ordinance Amendment Requiring Certification of Compliance with

   MEMORANDUM
  Agenda Item #: 1-3______
  Meeting Date: 01/25/18

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

THRU:  ANTON DAHLERBRUCH, CITY MANAGER

FROM:  SHERI REPP-LOADSMAN, PLANNING AND BUILDING DIRECTOR

SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION ITEMS FOR THE JOINT MEETING OF THE CITY
  COUNCIL, PLANNING COMMISSION AND PALOS VERDES
  HOMES ASSOCIATION

DATE:  JANUARY 25, 2018

The following are discussion items for the City Council, the Planning Commission, and Palos
Verdes Homes Association (PVHA) meeting of January 25, 2018.

  1. Status and Deliverables from the City/Palos Verdes Homes Association Ad Hoc
  Committee
  2. Consideration of Ordinance Amendment Requiring Certification of Compliance with
  CC&Rs
  3. Zoning Code Update for Accessory Dwelling Units and Junior Accessory Dwelling
  Units

For the discussion of each of these items, staff has summarized and framed the issues as
follows:

1. Status of Deliverables from the City/Palos Verdes Homes Association Ad Hoc
  Committee

  The topics discussed at the 2016 Joint meeting included:

  1.  Neighborhood Compatibility vs. View Preservation
  2.  Neighborhood Compatibility Comparison Chart – Garage and Average Size
  3.  Relative Jurisdiction
  4.  Vacation of City Rights-of-Ways/Parkways

  To address Neighborhood Compatibility, an Ad Hoc Committee was formed as a result of
  the 2016 Joint Meeting. The Ad Hoc Committee is comprised of two City Council
  Members, two Planning Commissioners, two Art Jury members, two PVHA Board
  members, and PVHA and City staff. At the July 27, 2017 Ad Hoc Committee meeting, it
  1  001
 was decided that a subcommittee be formed to focus on developing tools to clarify view
impacts and streamline the submittal process. To date, the Ad Hoc Committee is in the
process of completing the following:

  a. Residential development process flow,
  b. Impact assessment tool for Planning Commission review, and
  c. Database of Palos Verdes Estates residential project approvals (e.g. ridge
  heights, garage size, size of each floor, etc.).

Residential Development Process Flow
Currently, the applicant chooses which organization to start with first as it relates to
residential development and Neighborhood Compatibility. The applicant can choose to
start first with obtaining Art Jury preliminary approval and then following Art Jury
preliminary approval, obtaining Planning Commission approval or vice versa. The
subcommittee has been evaluating the development process and determining if there are
areas where the application process can be streamlined. The Committee has identified
several work products that are identical or similar between the PVHA and the City, such
as a site plan, floor plan, and elevations. In addition, the Committee has identified the
milestones each project has in order to move on to the next phase in the process. The
Committee discussed having shared applications and an electronic submittal system that
would allow both the PVHA and City to review the applications concurrently. Attached
is a presentation that Committee Member Dale Hoffman is in the process of completing
that identifies work products and outlines the development process for both the
PVHA/Art Jury and the City.

Impact Assessment Tool for Planning Commission Review
The Ad Hoc Committee discussed how mitigating impacts could potentially result in an
unfavorable architectural design and could affect the livability of the home. The
Committee noted that Planning Commissioners may view impacts differently than others.
Committee Member Michael Thomas recommended developing an impact assessment
tool to aid the Planning Commissioners in reviewing impacts of Neighborhood
Compatibility applications to adjacent neighbors. The assessment relates to the greatest
impacts of development projects, such as view, looming or massing, privacy, and
neighborhood character. The draft Impact Assessment Tool was created so that the
Planning Commissioners could make a more objective determination in reviewing
residential development applications. In addition, architects and the public can utilize
this tool to gain an understanding of what to expect with the process noting the major
areas of concern. A draft of the Impact Assessment Tool is attached.

Database of Residential Project Approvals
At the last Joint Meeting, the Neighborhood Compatibility Comparison Chart was
discussed. This chart is useful to the Planning Commission as it provides numerical data
in assessing neighborhood compatibility. Since the chart does not include the size of a
garage, it was noted that the chart could lead to a misleading floor area ratio in
comparison to surrounding neighbors. The source of the data used in the Neighborhood
Compatibility chart is from the Los Angeles County Assessor’s office and only includes
habitable floor area.

  2  002
   During the Ad Hoc Committee meetings, it was discussed that the Los Angeles County
  Assessor’s office could be calculating square footage differently than the City. For
  example, basements with a ceiling height of less than 7 ft. are not counted towards the
  floor area per the municipal code, however, it was unclear how the Assessor’s office
  calculates this area. The Ad Hoc Committee also recognized that there are other factors
  involved when reviewing compatibility, such as building height, gross floor area, size of
  second stories, plate heights, amount of grading, etc. In reviewing Neighborhood
  Compatibility applications, this information would be useful to the Commission to
  identify any trends in the neighborhood such as the average building height.

  The Ad Hoc Committee discussed having a database that would include information on
  past project approvals so the Commission, the applicant, and the public could compare
  projects within the surrounding neighborhood. The Ad Hoc Committee is evaluating
  how to design a database with this information and also the associated costs. Once that is
  determined, it will be brought back to the City Council and the Palos Verdes Homes
  Association to discuss the possible commitment of resources to establish this database.

  Discussion Topics:
  A. Are there benefits to streamlining the City and PVHA development process?
  Should applications, requirements for development plans and other details be
  similar in order to simplify the process? Should applicants be encouraged to
  apply to the PVHA before submittal to the Planning Commission?
  B. Should the Planning Commission attempt to create a standardized
  understanding of project impacts?  How should views (primary and
  secondary), privacy, looming/massing and neighborhood character impacts be
  determined and categorized (e.g. low, medium and high)?
  C. Discuss the feasibility for establishing a data base that includes information
  not collected by the Los Angeles County Assessor Office. What resources are
  needed to establish and maintain the data base?

2. Consideration of Ordinance Amendment Requiring Certification of
  Compliance with CC&Rs

  By practice, before the City issues a building permit, Palos Verdes Homes Association
  (PVHA) approval must be obtained. For example, plans for a residential development
  must be stamped by the PVHA before a City building permit is issued. The PVHA has
  suggested codifying the current practice of obtaining PVHA approval prior to permit
  issuance with a Certification of Compliance. The Certificate of Compliance would show
  that the project complies with the CC&R’s and PVHA Protective Restrictions and would
  be submitted to the City before a permit was issued.

  During the Ad Hoc Committee meetings, an example from the City of San Clemente
  Municipal Code was provided along with an example of the Certification of Compliance.
  The City of San Clemente’s municipal code and Certificate of Compliance is attached
  along with examples from other cities. In addition, during the Ad Hoc Committee
  meeting, it was discussed whether or not the Certification of Compliance would be
  applicable to both private property and public property, such as the City right-of-way and
  City Parklands. City staff noted to the Ad Hoc Committee that application to public
  right-of-way would likely not be recommended for improvements associated with

  3  003
   roadway design and installation of public utilities, including wireless telecommunication
  facilities.

  On October 26, 2017, the Ad Hoc Committee requested that the City Council consider
  potential adoption of an ordinance to require certification of compliance with the PVHA
  CC&Rs.

  Discussion Topics:
  A. Should the City formalize the current practice of requiring confirmation of PVHA
  approval before issuance of a building permit?
  B. There have been issues with the PVHA obtaining compliance from companies
  associated with wireless telecommunication facilities located within public rights-of-way.
  Questions have been raised by Crown Castle regarding the applicability of the CC&Rs to
  the public rights-of-way. Should any proposed ordinance apply to the public rights-of-
  way? If so, will the City withhold permits to all utility companies if PVHA authorization
  is not obtained?

3. Accessory Dwelling Units and Junior Accessory Dwelling Units

  The State of California recently adopted legislation that became effective January 1,
  2017, to encourage property owners to increase the supply of ADUs. Senate Bill 1069
  and Assembly Bill 2299 define an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) and authorize a local
  agency to provide, by ordinance, for the creation of second units in single family and
  multifamily residential zones, otherwise a local agency can default to state-law
  provisions. If a local agency decides to adopt its own ADU ordinance, then state law
  requires that the ordinance include specified provisions regarding areas where ADUs may
  be located, standards (including the imposition of parking), and lot density – among other
  things. The laws are currently in effect, so if cities do not pass ordinances refining how
  these senate and assembly bills are implemented, the state law is the overriding
  regulation, even if it is in conflict with local land use ordinances and general plans. The
  City is currently subject to the state law until such time that a local ordinance is adopted.

  The California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) must
  receive a copy of any ordinances within 60 days of adoption. HCD maintains a website
  providing information related to ADUs and links to the various city and county
  ordinances.

  The State law creates two types of ADUs – standard ADUs and Junior ADUs. A
  standard ADU is an attached or detached residential dwelling unit which shall include
  provisions for sleeping, cooking, eating and sanitation. It may also include an efficiency
  unit or manufactured home. ADUs are not intended for separate sale from a primary
  residence, meaning these units are intended to provide additional rental housing options.
  Junior ADUs are no larger than 500 square feet and located within an existing residential
  structure.

  The State’s ADU legislation includes the below components:

  •  Conversions of existing permitted residence or accessory structures are permitted.
  Resulting ADUs must comply with State requirements regarding habitable space.
  4  004
 •  Parking required for ADU– 1 per bedroom or 1 per unit, whichever is greater.
  a. Notwithstanding the above, no parking is required if
  i. ADU is located within ½ mile of public transit;
  ii. ADU is located within architecturally or historically significant historic district;
  iii. ADU is part of existing primary or accessory structure;
  iv. Where on-street parking permits required by not offered to ADU occupant; or
  v. Where there is car share vehicle located within one block of ADU.
•  Replacement parking for primary residence, if covered parking is demolished in
  conjunction with new ADU, may be located in any configuration on the same lot as
  the ADU, including, but not limited to as, covered spaces, uncovered spaces, tandem
  spaces or use of mechanical parking lifts.
•  No passageway (separation) shall be required between the ADU and the primary
  residence except as required by the Building Code.
•  No setback shall be required for the conversion of an existing garage and setback of
  no more than 5 ft. from side and rear lot lines shall be required for a new ADU
  constructed above a garage (if permitted in the zoning district).
•  All other ADU regulations, such as setbacks, size, etc. still apply.

Junior accessory dwelling units shall comply with the following requirements 1:
1. Be constructed within the existing walls of the structure and require the inclusion of
  an existing bedroom. A restriction on the size and attributes of the junior accessory
  dwelling unit that conforms to this section shall be recorded with the City as a deed
  restriction;
2. Include a separate entrance from the main entrance to the structure, with an interior
  entry to the main living area;
3. Include an efficiency kitchen, which shall include all of the following:
  (a) A sink with a maximum waste line diameter of 1.5 inches;
  (b) A cooking facility with appliances that do not require electrical service greater
  than 120 volts, or natural or propane gas; and
  (c) A food preparation counter and storage cabinets that are of reasonable size in
  relation to the size of the junior unit.

Areas of Discretion. ADUs can be avoided or allowed through a separate discretionary
process in areas with health and safety risks, such as high fire hazard areas. Designating
areas where ADUs are allowed should be approached primarily on health and safety
issues including water, sewer, traffic flow, and public safety. However, local standards
which unreasonably restrict the ability of homeowners to create an ADU would be
contrary to the intent of the legislation. Staff recommends consideration of the following:
• Carry over the existing development standards of the City’s former ordinance to the
  City’s new ADU ordinance.
  o Permitted for minimum lot size of 15,000 sq.ft.
  o Conditionally permitted for lot size of 10,000 sq.ft. to 14,999 sq.ft.
  o Detached ADU shall not exceed 700 sq.ft. unless approval of a conditional use
  permit
  o Maximum height of new construction not to exceed 18 feet.
• Consider allowing conditional approval of ADUs for properties with minimum 7,500
  sq.ft. or other size as deemed appropriate.

  5  005
   •  Consider amending the permitted size of an ADU to 150 sq.ft. minimum and 1,200
  sq.ft. maximum to be consistent with currently allowable size standards under state
  regulations.
  •  Prohibit or require conditional approval of ADUs in areas that have unsafe traffic or
  public safety conditions. Staff will coordinate with the Police Department and Los
  Angeles County Fire Department to identify potential areas where on- and off-street
  parking impacts and street conditions would impede the access of emergency vehicles
  and endanger public safety.

  Discussion Topics:
  A. Should the City establish specific development standards for ADUs that are not
  inconsistent with state law?
  B. The PVHA may have conflicts with state standards associated with ADUs (e.g.
  conversion of garage). How should the City and PVHA consider projects that may
  not obtain approvals from both organizations?
  C. Is there a benefit to allowing more ADUs and JADUs? Should there be community
  outreach to inform property owners of the ability to establish ADUs or JADUs?
  D.

   PLAN OF ATTACK (per 11/19/17)
The following are the steps planned in deriving the recommended flow to be used for
the PVE residential improvement projects approval process
  1) Review all of the products making up the overall process identifying those which are uniquely
  created by the PVE flow and are required by the PVHA as an input to complete one of its identified
  milestones
  2) Review all of the products making up the overall process identifying those which are uniquely
  created within the PVHA flow and are required by PVE as an input to complete one of its identified
  milestones
  3) These Giver/Receiver product sets represent constraining crossover tie-points between the two
  milestone flows as the product Receiver cannot proceed in that leg of the flow without the Giver
  having successfully generated the identified required product
  4) Analyze this family of critical crossover tie-points to synthesize an initial integrated process flow
  5) Use this initial flow as a strawman in discussions with George Sweeney and Criss Gunderson to
  ascertain their perspectives as working architects as to what the steps are in the typical activity flow
  of a residential Improvement project to ascertain if there are other practical aspects of the process
  that may also dictate critical crossover tie-points
  6) Adapt initial flow as appropriate to reflect results from Step 5 above
  7) Have Kimberly (PVHA) and Elizabeth (PVE) critique flow resulting from Step 6 above
  8) Incorporate strawman flow to reflect applicable comments from Step 7
  9) Present Step 8 result to Subgroup and incorporate comments
  10) Present recommended flow from Step 9 to full Ad hoc Subcommittee

  Obtaining a Building Permit

  1. Building Services permit application requires the following:

  Complete the three part application and sign where applicable (signature must be verified
  by office personnel). If you are applying as owner­builder, you must be the owner of
  record and complete part four of the multi part application. If property ownership was
  recently changed a copy of the grant deed may be required at time of application.
  When other than the owner or licensed contractor is applying for the permit, the second
  half of part four of the form must be completed, giving authority to sign as the owner's
  agent.
  An owner or their agent must sign a Deed Restriction Certificate declaring conformance
  with any applicable deed restrictions and/or CC&R's for subject property.
  If the property is within the architecturally controlled area of El Dorado Hills CSD or
  Cameron Park CSD, architectural approval of the plans from the district prior to permit
  issuance is a requirement. Failure to obtain approval may delay issuance of your permit.
  Check with your individual association for any restrictions that may affect your
  construction even though Building Services does not enforce these restrictions.
  Contractors acting as agent for the owner must have a current active California state
  contractors license, worker's compensation coverage, and a current El Dorado County

  square feet or more of land area, or is located within an Important Biological Corridor

  2. When served by a public water/sewer district other than El Dorado Irrigation District, you must
  submit proof of service from the district prior to permit issuance. When serviced by EID, they
  will review your project and approve electronically.

  3. When not served by public water/sewer, you must submit the perc test, septic design and well

  This plan must show the entire parcel and indicate and identify actual distances from all
  property lines and/or easements to structures, existing and proposed. Indicate all
  easements on the plan
  The plot plan shall also indicate distances between structures.
  Locate septic system(s), propane tank(s) and any other buildings.
  Indicate slope of lot.
  Contour lines (@ 1 ',2' or 5' vertical increments) must be shown for the building site
  and/or disturbed area and extend 20 feet beyond or to the property line, whichever is
  less.
  Similar contour lines must also be shown for the full length of a new driveway, if
  applicable.
  A profile for any new driveway on site. Also, public road to driveway improvements shown
  and dimensioned. Indicate the finished floor elevations for garage floor and first floor .
  The proposed method of compliance with State Fire Safe regulations regarding driveway
  slope, width, surface, turnouts and fuel modification shall be shown on these plans.
  Site Design Measures for Post Construction Storm Water Requirements.
  Any proposed grading is to be delineated in conformance with the County Design and
  Improvement Standards Manual.
  If the plot plan, drawn as required above, is too large to fit on a 24" x 36" sheet of paper,
  a SITE PLAN, drawn to a small scale, shall be provided which locates the area covered
  by the PLOT PLAN on the parcel.

  2. TITLE BLOCK giving: owner's name and mailing address, job site address, and assessor's
  parcel number. Include a summary of square footage identifying each proposed occupancy.
  3. FOUNDATION PLAN with details.
  4. FLOOR PLAN (fully dimensioned) illustrating proposed sizes and uses of rooms. Show braced
  wall panel locations or engineered shear walls (if applicable).
  5. FLOOR FRAMING PLAN with details (include deck framing if applicable).
  6. ROOF FRAMING PLAN. (Include the truss manufacturers specifications if a roof truss system
  is used. Must be reviewed and also signed by project engineer if applicable)

  7. ELEVATIONS including front, rear, and both sides.
  8. ELECTRICAL/MECHANICAL PLAN. This may be illustrated on the Floor Plan. Include a gas

  9. CALIFORNIA CEC TITLE 24 Energy Loss Report. Includes Form CF­1R and “Mandatory

  Please note: one additional floor plan is needed for the county Assessor's Office before

  An application missing any items will be deemed incomplete and the plan check will not

  affect application fees and codes since the operative date of application will be the date
